# Synthesis and Photodriven Hydrogenation of Tungsten Nitride Complexes Prepared from Dinitrogen Cleavage

**Authors:** Matthew V Pecoraro; Grace B Panetti; Junho Kim; Gabriele Hierlmeier; Paul J Chirik

**Affiliations:** 1 Department of Chemistry, Princeton University, Princeton, New Jersey 08544, United States

## Abstract

Oxidation of the Chatt-type tungsten dinitrogen compound, trans-(depe)2W­(N2)2 (depe = Et2PCH2CH2PEt2), with [(η5-C5H5)2Fe]­[BArF 4] (BArF 4 = B­(3,5-(CF3)2C6H3)4) resulted in isolation of [(depe)2WN]­[BArF 4], a rare example of a tungsten­(IV) nitride prepared from N2 cleavage. A bimetallic μ-N2 ditungsten intermediate supported by terminal N2 ligands was identified, and irradiation with visible light promoted dinitrogen cleavage and formation of [(depe)2WN]­[BArF 4]. Performing the analogous one-electron oxidation of the related tungsten dinitrogen compound, trans-(dppe)2W­(N2)2 (dppe = Ph2PCH2CH2PPh2), furnished the corresponding cationic, 17-electron tungsten dinitrogen complex, [(dppe)2W­(N2)2]­[BArF 4], that was characterized by X-ray diffraction and vibrational and EPR spectroscopies. The generation of [(dppe)2W­(N)]­[BArF 4] was observed in low yield from the in situ formed mixed N2-bridged compound, [(N2)­(depe)2W­(μ-N2)­W­(dppe)2(N2)]­[BArF 4]2, and was confirmed by independent synthesis using 1-azidoadamantane. Addition of ammonia or water to [(depe)2WN]­[BArF 4] resulted in formation of the cationic imide and hydroxide complexes, [(depe)2W­(NH)­(X)]­[BArF 4] (X = NH2, OH). Irradiation of [(depe)2WN]­[BArF 4] with 440 nm visible light in the presence of Ir­(ppy)3 (ppy = 2-phenylpyridine) under 4 atm of dihydrogen resulted in hydrogenation of the tungsten nitride to the cationic tungsten pentahydride, [(depe)2WH5]­[BArF 4], with the release of free ammonia in 21% yield, a rare example of ammonia generation from dinitrogen and dihydrogen from a well-defined tungsten nitride.

Keywords: tungsten, dinitrogen cleavage, terminal nitride, hydrogenation, mechanism

## Introduction

The synthesis of ammonia from its elements with molecular compounds is a long-standing challenge in synthetic chemistry. While the industrial Haber–Bosch process has enabled the widespread distribution of ammonia-based fertilizers for over a century, replicating N2 hydrogenation with molecular compounds may provide fundamental insights into N–H bond formation and enable more energy efficient and carbon-neutral reactions. Although N2 coordination and cleavage by organometallic and coordination compounds is well precedented, − subsequent N–H bond formation from the resulting metal nitrides has proven challenging, especially when using H2 as the hydrogen atom source. − The formation of strong MN bonds after dinitrogen cleavage consequently results in low N–H bond dissociation free energies, often below the threshold for spontaneous formation of dihydrogen. Alternative strategies, such as the hydrogenation of activated side-on metal dinitrogen compounds and protonation from coordinated dihydrogen, have been used for N–H bond formation and ammonia synthesis. One notable example was reported by Hidai and co-workers, where a ruthenium η2-dihydrogen complex was used to protonate a Chatt-type tungsten dinitrogen compound, resulting in 55% yield of free ammonia (Scheme a, left).

*1: Dinitrogen Hydrogenation and Cleavage by Homogeneous Group 6 Metal Compounds*

Our laboratory has demonstrated the application of visible light in promoting N–H bond formation from terminal metal nitrides. Initial studies demonstrated that ruthenium photocatalysts in combination with dihydroacridine were effective for the hydrogenation of terminal manganese nitrides to produce up to 80% yield of free ammonia. A subsequent report established that blue-light irradiation of dihydroacridine in the absence of a metal photocatalyst was also effective for ammonia synthesis from manganese nitrides with ammonia yields of up to 85% under optimized conditions.

Ammonia synthesis was also demonstrated in the photodriven hydrogenation of the N2-derived molybdenum nitride, [(depe)2MoN]­[BArF 4], in the presence of the piano-stool iridium hydride, (η5-C5Me5)­Ir­(ppy)­H (Scheme a, middle). Use of fac-Ir­(ppy)3 as the photocatalyst and additional reaction optimization resulted in near quantitative yields of 87% of ammonia and enabled a synthetic cycle whereby the resulting cationic molybdenum pentahydride was used to promote N2 cleavage and regeneration of [(depe)2MoN]­[BArF 4] (Scheme a, right). Ultimately, superstoichiometric ammonia generation in 112% yield was accomplished after three synthetic cycles.

Phosphine-supported group 6 transition metal dinitrogen complexes were first studied by Chatt and further investigated by Hidai. These compounds exhibit weakly activated, end-on bound dinitrogen ligands that, in certain cases, yield ammonia when treated with strong acid. In 2019, Masuda and co-workers reported that the addition of a one-electron ferrocenium oxidant to trans-(depe)2Mo­(N2)2 promoted dinitrogen cleavage to furnish the corresponding molybdenum nitride, [(depe)2MoN]­[BArF 4], in 62% yield (Scheme b). One-electron oxidation of the Mo(0), d 6 complex formed a μ-N2 bimetallic Mo­(I) dinitrogen compound with 10 π-electrons that achieves the geometric and electronic requirements to access the “zigzag” transition state and promote N2 cleavage.

While dinitrogen cleavage with molybdenum compounds is well precedented, analogous reactivity with tungsten remains rare (Scheme c). In 2015, Sita and co-workers reported the synthesis of a terminal nitride derived from dinitrogen on a tungsten center. In this report, a tungsten nitride chloride supported by pentamethylcyclopentadiene and ethanimidam-ide ligands was accessed after the addition of trimethylsilyl chloride to a side-on bound bridging dinitrogen compound. In 2019, Schneider and co-workers described that the protonation of a MACHO-type ligand in a chloro tungsten bridging dinitrogen compound triggered the splitting of dinitrogen and yielded the terminal nitride under certain conditions. Both the photodriven and the reversible thermal cleavage of N2 were observed in a related tungsten carbonyl derivative. Most recently, Ballmann and Eberle have reported the cleavage of dinitrogen from a tungsten complex bearing a 2,2′-(tBu2As)2-substituted diphenylacetylene chelate.

Reports of the hydrogenation of molecular N2-derived transition metal nitrides with H2 as the terminal reductant to yield ammonia are uncommon in the literature, − with no reports of isolated tungsten nitride compounds exhibiting such reactivity. Recent reports have described catalytic ammonia formation from N2-derived tungsten compounds using SmI2/H2O as well as electrochemical methods that rely on proton-coupled electron transfer (PCET) mediators. In addition to providing fundamental insights into dinitrogen cleavage, the synthesis of a tungsten congener of an N2-derived molybdenum nitride is of interest to determine the limits of the photodriven hydrogenation strategy for strong metal–ligand multiple bonds. Tungsten nitride bonds are anticipated to be stronger than their molybdenum counterparts due to the established trends in bond strengths among transition metals.

Here, we describe a rare example of dinitrogen cleavage from a Chatt-type tungsten dinitrogen complex by one-electron oxidation. An intermediate ditungsten compound with one bridging and two terminal dinitrogen ligands was observed that required photolysis to promote N2 scission and formation of the terminal tungsten nitride, [(depe)2WN]­[BArF 4]. This metal nitride undergoes photodriven hydrogenation to yield ammonia and a cationic pentahydride in the presence of the photocatalyst Ir­(ppy)3, demonstrating the ability of this approach to cleave strong metal–ligand multiple bonds.

## Results and Discussion

### Synthesis of a Tungsten­(IV) Nitride by Oxidative Dinitrogen Cleavage

Our studies commenced with the synthesis and isolation of the Chatt-type tungsten dinitrogen compound, (depe)2W­(N2)2 (W1). Addition of [(η5-C5H5)2Fe]­[BArF 4] to a diethyl ether solution of W1 resulted in formation of a yellow, paramagnetic, X-band EPR-silent tungsten product (Scheme ). The diethyl ether solution infrared spectrum exhibited a strong band at 1990 cm–1, consistent with a terminal N2 stretch. As expected from oxidation, this band has a higher frequency than the value of 1915 cm–1 for W1. The Raman spectrum recorded in diethyl ether solution exhibited an intense band centered at 1334 cm–1, assigned to the symmetric stretch of a bridging dinitrogen ligand. This value is comparable to those previously reported for bridging group 6 transition metal dinitrogen complexes, including [(tBuPNP)­MoCl]2(μ-N2) (νN2 = 1343 cm–1, tBuPNP = N­(CH2CH2PtBu2)2) and [(depe)2Mo]2(μ-N2) (νN2 = 1292 cm–1). Paramagnetic W1 is NMR silent, and no change was observed upon cooling a THF-d 8 solution to −50 °C. Likewise, a THF-d 8 solution magnetic moment (Evans method) of 2.0(6) μB was measured at 23 °C, lower than the spin-only value expected for two noninteracting d 1 ions likely due to either spin interaction through the μ-N2 ligand or spin–orbit coupling.

*2: One-Electron-Induced Cleavage of Dinitrogen by (depe)2W­(N2)2*

Based on the spectroscopic data, the product of the oxidation of W1 was assigned as the dicationic, bimetallic tungsten­(I) compound with one bridging and two terminal dinitrogen ligands, [(depe)2W­(N2)]2(μ-N2) (W2, Scheme ). This product is related to the intermediate proposed by Masuda and co-workers based on in situ resonance Raman experiments on the corresponding molybdenum derivative with the difference being the tungsten congener having terminal dinitrogen ligands.

Although no change to THFor Et2O solutions of W2 were observed upon heating to 60 °C for 12 h, irradiation of a diethyl ether solution for 15 min with white LEDs either under dinitrogen or static vacuum led to complete conversion of the starting material. A color change from yellow to purple to dark red was observed, and the cationic tungsten nitride, [(depe)2WN]­[BArF 4] W3, was isolated in 91% yield (Scheme ). It is likely that visible light promotes the dissociation of the terminal N2 ligands to achieve the requisite coordination number and geometry to promote dinitrogen cleavage. The distinction between photoinduced N2 dissociation in tungsten complexes and thermal loss in corresponding molybdenum congeners has been previously reported in Chatt–Hidai-type group 6 complexes. The 31P NMR spectrum of W3 in THF-d 8 exhibited a singlet at 67.9 ppm with 183W satellites (1 J PW = 151 Hz), similar to the value of 64.4 ppm reported by Masuda for the molybdenum congener.

Vapor diffusion of pentane into a concentrated diethyl ether solution of W3 at −35 °C produced dark-red crystals suitable for X-ray diffraction, and the solid-state structure confirmed the formation of W3 (Figure ). The WN bond length of 1.675(7) Å is comparable to the value of 1.646(6) Å reported for the molybdenum compound. W3 is a rare example of a crystallographically characterized W­(IV) nitride , and is uniquely prepared by oxidative N2 cleavage.

Extension of oxidative dinitrogen cleavage to another Chatt-type tungsten dinitrogen compound was also explored to determine the generality of the transformation. Treatment of trans-(dppe)2W­(N2)2 (W4) with one equivalent of [(η5-C5H5)2Fe]­[BArF 4] resulted in rapid formation of a new paramagnetic tungsten product. The diethyl ether solution infrared spectrum ether contained a strong band at 2010 cm–1, assigned as a terminal N2 stretch. No bands assignable to bridging dinitrogen ligands were located in the corresponding diethyl ether solution Raman spectrum. Based on the vibrational data, the product of oxidation of W4 was assigned as the cationic tungsten­(I) bis­(dinitrogen) compound W5 (Scheme ).

*3: Oxidation of (dppe)2W­(N2)2 to Form [(dppe)2W­(N2)2]­[BArF 4]*

The spectroscopic data and structural assignment are consistent with a report by Colquhoun and Head, where the synthesis of cationic trans-[(dppe)2W­(N2)2] complexes supported by I3 –, FeCl4 –, and tetracyanoethene (TCNE) anions was described, each with a characteristic dinitrogen stretching frequency at 1988 cm–1. The X-band EPR spectrum of W5 in 2-MeTHF glass at 20 K exhibited a rhombic signal with g-values of 2.76, 2.05, and 1.30, consistent with a S = 1/2, low-spin tungsten­(I) compound (Figure a). A values of 200 and 40 G for hyperfine coupling of 31P and 14N nuclei, respectively, provided the best fit. The solution-state magnetic susceptibility of W5 was determined by Evan’s method in THF-d 8 to be 1.1(8) μB, consistent with a low-spin W­(I) complex.

The solid-state structure of W5 was determined by X-ray diffraction using single crystals obtained from vapor diffusion of pentane into a concentrated diethyl ether solution at room temperature (Figure b). These data confirm the formation of an idealized octahedral, 17-electron tungsten bis­(dinitrogen) complex, [trans-(dppe)2W­(N2)2]­[BArF 4]. The NN bond length of 1.134(9) Å, is statistically indistinguishable from the value of 1.126(15) Å reported for the neutral analogue, W4. The similarity in NN bond distances is anticipated as oxidation results in loss of an electron from an essentially nonbonding t 2g -type orbital. Likewise, the W–P bond lengths of 2.5077(15) and 2.5034(15) Å are similar to those reported in W4 at 2.452(3), 2.466(3), 2.455(3), and 2.444(3) Å.

Attempts to promote N2 cleavage from W5 by allowing the compound to stand at ambient temperature for 24 h or heating to 60 °C in THF were unsuccessful and produced no reaction. Irradiation of a diethyl ether solution of the compound with white LEDs or ultraviolet light for 12 h also produced no reaction. Because W5 is monomeric, it is likely that the phenyl substituents sterically prevent formation of the bridged dinitrogen intermediate required for N2 cleavage.

The desired cationic tungsten­(IV) nitride, [(dppe)2WN]+ (W6), was previously proposed by Tuczek and co-workers following the protonation of the tungsten dialkyhydrazido complex, (dppe)2W­(N-NC5H10), with HLutBPh4 with concomitant release of piperidine. The independent synthesis of W6 was also accomplished by the addition of 1-azidoadamantane to a diethyl ether solution of W5 (Scheme ). The 31P­{1H} NMR spectrum of W6 in diethyl ether exhibits a singlet at 72.86 ppm with a characteristic 1 J PW coupling of 159 Hz. A singlet at 836 ppm was observed in the 15N NMR spectrum of W6- 15 N with 183W satellites of 25 Hz.

The synthesis of W3 by dinitrogen cleavage and the isolation of W5 and its inertness toward such reactivity supports the pathway for N2-derived tungsten nitride formation illustrated in Scheme . One-electron oxidation of trans-(P2)2W­(N2)2 results in formation of the corresponding 17-electron, cationic tungsten bis­(dinitrogen) compound. With appropriately sized phosphine substituents, dissociation of an N2 ligand enables formation of the bimetallic μ2-dinitrogen intermediate with two terminal N2 ligands. Unlike molybdenum where these ligands are thermally labile, irradiation with visible light is required with tungsten to access the requisite “zigzag” transition state en route to the W­(IV) nitride product.

*5: Proposed Mechanism for One-Electron Oxidation-Induced Dinitrogen Cleavage*

A mixing experiment was conducted to evaluate the feasibility of the proposed mechanism. While the phenyl substituents in W5 were too large to form the bimetallic intermediate, mixing the dppe-supported tungsten compound with the depe variant may enable formation of the requisite μ2-dinitrogen ligand. Three equivalents of W1 were added to one equivalent of W5 generated in situ, followed by the addition of three equivalents of [Cp2Fe]­[BArF 4] in THF-d 8 (Scheme ). An excess of W1 was added due to homodimerization and irreversible cleavage of the nonmixed bridge W2 competing with potential formation of the mixed-bridge compound. Irradiation of the reaction, with white LEDs, yielded both tungsten nitrides, as judged by 31P NMR spectroscopy, indicating the intermediacy of the mixed-bridge compound in the reaction.

### Reactivity of the N2-Derived Tungsten­(IV) Nitride

The reactivity of W3 with water, ammonia, and dihydrogen was explored. While optimizing the synthesis of W3, it was determined that several undesired byproducts were removed by performing the photodriven cleavage in silylated glassware, consistent with the oxophilicity of the tungsten intermediates and products. This observation motivated experiments to determine the reactivity of W3 with H2O under controlled conditions.

One equivalent of water was added as a dilute stock solution in diethyl ether to a solution of W3, resulting in a color change from red to yellow, signaling formation of the cationic imido hydroxide compound, [(depe)2W­(NH)­(OH)]­[BArF 4] (W7, Scheme a). The THF-d 8 31P NMR spectrum exhibited a singlet at 33.80 ppm while broad peaks were located at 5.77 and 0.42 ppm in the 1H NMR spectrum corresponding to the protons in the imido and hydroxide ligands, respectively. Both O–H and N–H stretches were observed in the solid-state (KBr) infrared spectrum at 3696 and 3417 cm–1, respectively. A deuterium-enriched sample was prepared using D2O, and it exhibited near identical shifts in the Et2O 2H NMR spectrum and isotopically shifted bands in the solid-state (KBr) IR spectrum at 2725 and 2542 cm–1.

*7: Reactivity of [(depe)2W­(N)]­[BArF 4] with Water and Ammonia*

The addition of NH3 to W3 was also explored. An excess of ammonia (∼10 equiv) was added to a THF-d 8 solution of W3, and a color change from red to yellow was observed, accompanied by complete conversion of the starting material (Scheme b). Analysis of the reaction mixture by 31P NMR spectroscopy in THF-d 8 revealed formation of a singlet at 29.65 ppm. This observation along with the appearance of broadened 1H NMR resonances at −1.25 and 6.61 ppm in a 2:1 ratio was consistent with formation of [(depe)2W­(NH)­(NH2)] (W8). When the reaction was repeated using 15NH3 and natural abundance nitrogen in W3, the broadened 1H NMR resonance at −1.25 ppm appeared as a doublet of quintets (1 J NH = 65.9 Hz,3 J PH = 5.5 Hz), supporting coupling of the proton to the 15N nuclei and the four 31P nuclei bound to tungsten. The lack of a broadened peak between the doublet of quintets implies that there is no self-tautomerization between the protons of the amido and imido ligands. It is likely that the broadening of the proton resonances in the natural abundance sample is a result of the quadrupolar 14N nucleus. Likewise, the lack of resolution on the broadened imido resonance further corroborates the absence of self-tautomerization. The 15N NMR spectrum, indirectly detected using an 15N–1H HSQC experiment, displayed only one resonance, observed at 21.3 ppm relative to NH3, which correlated with the amido 1H resonance. When ND3 was used, the resonances assigned to the amido and imido ligands on the 1H NMR were no longer observed with near identical peaks being observed in the 2H NMR spectrum. Notably, W8 converted back to W3 after extended exposure to active vacuum, demonstrating that the addition of ammonia is reversible.

Given previous reports of the hydrogenation of its molybdenum congener, [(depe)2Mo­(N)]­[BArF 4], the hydrogenation of W3 was explored to determine if established methods are capable of promoting the hydrogenation of the strong WN triple bond (Scheme ). Using the conditions previously optimized for the molybdenum congener, irradiation of a THF solution of W3 in the presence of 2.5 mol % of Ir­(ppy)3 with 440 nm blue LEDs under 4 atm of H2 produced NH3 in 21% yield. Control experiments established the decomposition of W3 upon irradiation in the absence of Ir­(ppy)3 without generation of ammonia. The yield of ammonia was determined by vacuum transfer of the volatiles after the reaction to a side-arm flask containing excess 2 M HCl in diethyl ether to trap ammonia as ammonium chloride. Performing the hydrogenation in THF-d 8 with H2 gas produced NH3 exclusively as judged by trapping with BH3 and analysis by NMR spectroscopy.

*8: Photodriven Hydrogenation of [(depe)2W­(N)]­[BArF 4] with Ir­(ppy)3*

Analysis of the nonvolatile components by 31P NMR spectroscopy revealed a peak centered at 50.93 ppm corresponding to the tungsten pentahydride derivative, [(depe)2WH5]­[BArF 4] (W9). This product, formed in 61% yield, also exhibited a quintet (2 J PH = 30.7 Hz) at −4.12 ppm in the 1H NMR spectrum, consistent with hydride ligands split by four equivalent 31P nuclei. Independent synthesis of W9 was accomplished by first synthesizing the neutral polyhydride, (depe)2WH4, by photolysis of W1 in the presence of dihydrogen. Protonation of (depe)2WH4 by addition of one equivalent [H­(OEt2)2]­[BArF 4] in THF-d 8 generated NMR signals identical to those observed following the hydrogenation of W3. Attempts to induce N2 cleavage from W9 as was reported for the molybdenum congener either thermally or photochemically have been unsuccessful.

No remaining resonances in the 31P NMR spectrum of the hydrogenation reaction account for greater than 10% of the reaction mixture. W7 was observed in 3% yield, and W8 was not observed. Two doublets at 40.32 and 38.96 ppm were observed in 9 and 8% yields and are assigned as [(depe)2W­(NH)­(F)]­[BArF 4] and [(depe)2W­(O)­(F)]­[BArF 4], resulting from photodegradation of the BArF 4 anion. Free depe represents an additional 8% of the observed 31P containing products. Digestion of the nonvolatile mixtures with H2SO4 failed to produce additional ammonium salts.

The hydrogenolysis reactivity of W6 was also investigated to assess the influence of ligand environment on nitride reduction. Upon irradiation with blue LEDs under four atmospheres of dihydrogen, only trace amounts of ammonia were detected. The nonvolatile components of the reaction mixture were intractable with no spectroscopic evidence for hydrogenation of the tungsten nitride. It is likely that the increased susceptibility of W6 toward cyclometalation under photolytic conditions is responsible for the lack of productive hydrogenation reactivity. These observations are consistent with prior observations of cyclometalation in dppe-supported tungsten complexes when exposed to irradiative and hydrogenative conditions.

Notably, the hydrogenation of W3 demonstrates that a bisphosphine-supported tungsten­(IV) nitride undergoes hydrogenation to generate ammonia and (depe)2W­(H)5 cationic products upon photoirradiation with Ir­(ppy)3. This represents a rare example of ammonia generation from dihydrogen and a well-defined terminal tungsten nitride and demonstrates that even the recalcitrant WN bond is amenable to hydrogenation under photoirradiative conditions.

## Conclusions

The W­(IV) nitride [(depe)2W­(N)]­[BArF 4] (W3) was generated by the cleavage of dinitrogen following one-electron oxidation and visible-light irradiation of (depe)2W­(N2)2 (W1), representing a rare example of dinitrogen cleavage leading to the formation of a W­(IV) nitride. A dinitrogen bridging bimetallic intermediate (W2) was spectroscopically characterized and identified as en route to nitride generation. While this reactivity was facile in the case of W1, when the depe ligands are replaced by dppe ligands (W4), N2 cleavage was not observed. Instead, oxidation resulted in the formation of a 17-electron monometallic W­(I) compound (W5), which is unable to form the requisite bridging intermediate to cleave dinitrogen due to steric repulsion. The corresponding nitride to W4 has been independently synthesized using 1-azidoadamantane as the nitrogen source. A mechanism for one-electron oxidation-induced dinitrogen splitting is proposed and was probed through the formation of a mixed bridged compound. Hydrogenation of the N2-derived nitride W3 resulted in the release of free ammonia with concomitant generation of a tungsten pentahydride cation compound, W9. This represents a rare example of ammonia generation from dinitrogen with dihydrogen as a terminal reductant, and the first time this reactivity has been observed on a well-defined tungsten nitride.

# Photodriven Ammonia Synthesis from Manganese Nitrides: Photophysics and Mechanistic Investigations

KEYWORDS proton coupled electron transfer, ammonia, manganese, nitride, ultrafast spectroscopy, mechanism, acridine

ABSTRACT:  Ammonia synthesis from N,N,O,O-supported manganese (V) nitrides and 9,10-dihydroacridine using protoncoupled electron transfer and visible light irradiation in the absence of precious metal photocatalysts is described. While the reactivity of the nitride correlated with increased absorption of blue light, excited-state lifetimes determined by transient absorption were on the order of picoseconds. This eliminated excited state manganese nitrides as responsible for bimolecular N–H bond formation. Spectroscopic measurements on the hydrogen source, dihydroacridine, demonstrated that photooxidation of 9,10-dihydroacridine was necessary for productive ammonia synthesis. Transient absorption and pulse radiolysis data for dihydroacridine provided evidence for the presence of intermediates with weak E–H bonds, including the dihydroacridinium radical cation and both isomers of monohydroacridine radical but notably these intermediates were unreactive towards hydrogen atom transfer and net N–H bond formation. Additional optimization of the reaction conditions using higher photon flux, resulted in higher rates of the ammonia production from the manganese(V) nitrides due to increased activation of the dihydroacridine.

## INTRODUCTION

Metal nitrides are of broad interest due to applications in materials science and coordination chemistry.1 Notably, terminal transition metal nitrides serve as the nitrogen source in both atom transfer and ammonia synthesis chemistry.2 However, the thermodynamic stability of most isolable metal nitrides results in weak N–H bonds in the corresponding imido complexes.3 One approach to overcoming this energetic limitation is the use of separate proton and electron sources that by formation of stoichiometric byproducts incur large chemical overpotentials.3c,4

Alternatively, molecules containing weak element-hydrogen (E–H) bonds are attractive for forming N–H bonds from thermodynamically stable metal nitrides. Those with BDFEs less than 50 kcal mol-1 are of particular interest to promote additional chemistry.5 Various alternative approaches have been explored to activate molecules to reduce BDFEs and enable productive H-atom transfer chemistry. Strategies include coordination to a metal (coordination-induced bond weakening), photon absorption, redox chemistry or H-atom transfer events (Scheme 1b).5b,6 While irradiation with visible light has been posited, photoredox methods have dominated as an effective strategy for generating reactive intermediates with low effective BDFEs.7 These approaches have been used extensively for the formation and cleavage of E–H bonds through protoncoupled electron transfer (PCET) with implications in biochemistry and organic chemistry and activation of metalligand multiple bonds.5

The application of photoinduced PCET to generate weak E– H bonds for subsequent N–H bond formation with metal nitrides has been demonstrated as a distinct route for ammonia synthesis (Scheme 2A).3c Blue light irradiation of salensupported manganese nitrides in the presence of a ruthenium photocatalyst, acid and 9,10-dihydroacridine (H2Acr) as the terminal reductant was effective for ammonia synthesis.6g,8 Related work by Nishibayashi and coworkers demonstrated catalytic ammonia synthesis using a PCP pincer molybdenum complex, an iridium photocatalyst, and H2Acr.9 Peters and coworkers have also applied this approach to catalytic ammonia synthesis using a PNP pincer molybdenum complex, an iridium photocatalyst, and a Hantzsch ester as the stoichiometric H-atom source.10 In all of the reported examples, ammonia formation was observed, albeit in significantly lower yields in the absence of the precious metal photocatalyst. These observations raise questions as to the nature of the photoactive compound in solution responsible for N–H bond formation. Despite extensive photophysical measurements on terminal metal oxides11 and metal alkylidynes,12 related studies on the photophysics of metal nitrides are comparatively rare and principally focused on luminescence.13

The use of acridine derivatives and Hantzsch esters as hydrogen atom donors is also well established. Here we describe the exploration of the origin and mechanism of light-driven ammonia formation from manganese nitrides in the absence of a precious metal photocatalyst (Scheme 2B). The synthesis and isolation of multiple manganese nitrides is reported and their ground state spectroscopy and electrochemical data are described. The BDFEs of previously proposed intermediates indicate that the formation of either the manganese (IV) imido or acridine radical are responsible for ammonia formation. Using transient absorption pump-probe spectroscopy, the lifetimes of salen-supported manganese nitrides were measured and determined to be significantly shorter than the required lifetime to engage in diffusion-based reaction chemistry. Instead, light absorption of acridine derivatives is responsible for the initiation of N–H bond formation and subsequent ammonia production.

One hypothesis for the photoproduction of ammonia in the absence of a precious metal photocatalyst relies on excitation of the manganese nitride by visible light to engage in subsequent N–H bond formation. Because only one example of a salen-supported manganese nitride (MnN-1) was examined for ammonia synthesis,6g,8 ligand modifications were explored to systematically evaluate the role of blue light absorption. Photophysical Studies of Manganese Nitrides. To evaluate the pathway involving reactivity from the excited state of the manganese nitride, the excited state lifetimes of each complex was measured using pump-probe transient absorption (TA) spectroscopy. Using a 430 nm pulse to best replicate the conditions of the ammonia synthesis reaction, signals were observed for all four manganese nitride derivatives. However, the signals that were observed did not exceed 100 ps (Figure 3, Figures S58–S73). All of the manganese nitrides studied display bleaching of signals observed in the ground state electronic absorption spectra. In addition, new excited state absorbances (ESAs) were detected at lower energies. The observation of new, red-shifted absorbances without the formation of a new structure is diagnostic of a vibrationally hot ground state, rather than an electronic excited state.22 No evidence for an observable excited state was obtained, consistent with the excited state lifetime being shorter than the limit of the experiment (< 100 fs). These lifetimes were also invariant in the solvents examined (THF, PhCF3, and 1:1 THF:iPrOH) and inconsistent with the observed experimental solvent effect. Relevant to the ammonia synthesis reaction, such short lifetimes are incompatible with pathways involving a bimolecular reaction between a photoexcited manganese nitride and H2Acr in solution.

## CONCLUSION

By tuning the ligand supporting a manganese(V) nitride, ammonia synthesis superior to that observed with precious metal photocatalysts has been observed. The mechanistic investigation led by TA spectroscopy established that this ligand effect had little impact on the photophysics of the metal nitride but instead was correlated with the ability of the compound to accept electrons. Accepting electrons either by the ligand or the solvent is pivotal towards the activation of the source of the proton and the electron, H2Acr. Oxidation of H2Acr results in the production of H2Acr+•, HAcr• and HAcr•′, which were all observed by TA experiments, and all contain weak E–H bonds, but are not observed to engage in hydrogen atom transfer reactions. Only H2Acr+• was shown to be capable of reacting with MnN and only through electron transfer. This work is expected to have implications for future work into photodriven ammonia synthesis.

ABSTRACT: The synthesis and characterization of pentamethylcyclopentadienyl iron complexes bearing the redox non-innocent α-diimine (N,Nʹ-dimesitylbutane-2,3-diimine, MesDI) and α-iminopyridine (N-mesityl(pyridin-2-yl)ethanimine MesPI) ligands were explored. The resulting iron compounds were characterized by paramagnetic 1H NMR spectroscopy, magnetic susceptibility measurements, zero-field 57Fe Mössbauer spectroscopy, low-temperature EPR spectroscopy, and cyclic voltammetry. The combined spectroscopic, structural and DFT computational data supported low-spin iron(III) compounds  (SFe  = ½) with -acidic, formally doubly-reduced chelating ligands.

## INTRODUCTION

Organometallic metalloradicals are of interest due to their ability to undergo unique covalent bond activation modes through rapid electronic reorganization.1 Among many types of fundamental transformations, 2-5 homolytic H2 cleavage to furnish metal hydride complexes has been extensively studied in the context of catalytic reduction of various substrates.6-10 Classical examples include organometallic compounds with piano-stool geometries having η5- cyclopentadienyl ligands.6 Hoff and co-workers first reported kinetic parameters for H2 homolysis with (η5- C5H5)Cr(CO)3• metalloradical species,11-12 and the Norton group has revisited the system and provided in-depth mechanistic details.13 Key to this reactivity was the generation of relatively stable 17-electron chromium radicals from its dimeric form.

Our group has been interested in coordination compounds that undergo proton-coupled electron transfer with molecular hydrogen as the terminal reductant, principally in the context of ammonia synthesis. Group 8 and 9 transition metal hydrides have been the most commonly studied due to their low acidity and propensity to promote the activation of H2 gas. The piano-stool rhodium hydride, (η5- C5Me5)Rh(κ2-L,X)H (L,X = 2-phenylpyridine), first reported by Norton and coworkers in 2014,14 has been applied to the catalytic synthesis of ammonia from titanium-amido 15 and manganese-nitride complexes, 16 respectively. Key to the success of this catalyst was regeneration of the Rh–H bond from the putative 17-electron rhodium radical and H2. In support of a metalloradical intermediate, an EPR-active product was detected following H-atom abstraction of the Rh–H bond with (2,2,6,6-Tetramethylpiperidin-1-yl)oxyl

Replacing precious metals with more Earth abundant ones in catalysts for H2 activation and subsequent hydrogen atom transfer is a long-standing goal and important for improving the overall sustainability and eventual scalability of such reactions. Along these lines, the isoelectronic and potentially isolable iron congeners of the ruthenium hydrides were targeted.20 Specifically, the synthesis of (η5- C5Me5)Fe(κ2-N,Nʹ)H derivatives was explored, and during the course of these investigations, reliable routes to isolable 17-electron iron metalloradicals were discovered. Various spectroscopic techniques in conjunction with computational studies support low-spin ferric compounds with metal-centered radicals and dianionic ligand redox noninnocent ligands.

RESULTS AND DISCUSSION Synthesis and Characterization of Piano-Stool Iron Complexes. Initial synthetic efforts focused on the preparation of (η5-C5Me5)Fe(κ2-N,Nʹ)Cl as the ruthenium congeners are the precursors to the corresponding hydrides (Scheme 2).14, 17-18 Potentially redox-active -diimine (DI) and pyridine(imine) (PI) ligands were selected because of their synthetic accessibility, crystallinity and success in supporting ruthenium hydride catalysts. Addition of two equivalent of Li[C5Me5] to a THF solution of (MesDI)FeCl2 resulted in formation of a dark yellow reaction mixture. Subsequent extraction of the iron product into toluene afforded a single paramagnetic product, as judged by 1H NMR spectroscopy. The benzene-d6 1H NMR spectrum recorded at ambient temperature exhibited paramagnetically broadened and shifted resonances ranging from −26 to −6 ppm, where a diagnostic [C5Me5] peak was located at −17.4 ppm (Figure S1). Single crystals suitable for X-ray diffraction were obtained from a saturated solution of the isolated compound in pentane stored at -30 °C. A representation of the solid-state structure of Fe1 is presented in Figure 1a and establishes the formation of a piano-stool iron compound that lacks a chloride ligand. This product was also obtained in 90% isolated yield from addition of two equivalents of Li[C5Me5] to (MesDI)FeCl2. Thus, addition of Li[C5Me5] to (κ2-N,Nʹ)FeCl2 resulted in loss of two chlorides, one from reduction and the other from salt metathesis. Similar reactivity was observed in a (β-diketiminato)chromium system, where two equivalents of Na[C5H5] was used to furnish (η5-C5Me5)Cr(β- diketiminato) compounds.21

Having achieved the formal reduction to Fe1, alternative synthetic routes to the compound were sought. Photolysis of a benzene solution of [(η5-C5Me5)Fe(CO)2]2 (Fp*2) and MesDI under static vacuum resulted in formation of a paramagnetic compound with NMR signals consistent with Fe1, arising from photodissociation of carbon monoxide from Fp* followed by coordination of the -diimine ligand. Extraction with pentane, followed by recrystallization furnished Fe1 in 30% yield. The photochemical route provided lower yield, potentially due to slow CO release under blue light irradiation.22

Various spectroscopic measurements were used to further characterize the spin state and overall electronic structure of the complexes. Magnetic properties of the bulk samples were measured by a magnetic susceptibility balance and in benzene solution by the Evans method. Effective solid-state magnetic moments of 2.3(1) and 2.4(1) μB were measured for Fe1 and Fe2, respectively, at 23 ºC and are in agreement with the benzene-d6 solution values of 2.5(2) μB for Fe1 and 2.4(2) μB for Fe2. While slightly higher than the spin-only value for one unpaired electron, these values are most consistent with S = 1/2 ground states. Variable temperature 1H NMR studies in toluene-d8 demonstrated that the proton resonances of Fe1 and Fe2 obeyed the Curie be-

havior (δ ∝ T-1) between 243 and 298 K (Figure S3 and S4), consistent with simple paramagnetic behavior.

Zero-field 57Fe Mössbauer spectra were recorded in the solid state at 80 K, and the fitting parameters from the least square regression analysis are depicted in Figure 2. The spectroscopic parameters observed for Fe1 and Fe2 were indistinguishable: isomer shifts (δ) of 0.41 and 0.48 mm/s, and quadrupole splitting (|ΔEQ|) of 0.58 and 0.57 mm/s were measured. For Fe2, <5% of an iron impurity was detected (red line, Figure 2b). The observation of essentially the same peak shape and fitting parameters support that the electronic structures of these two compounds are indistinguishable. Isomer shifts in the range of 0.4-0.5 mm/s are consistent with low-spin ferric compounds,29 and indeed, quantum chemical simulation of Mössbauer parameters by DFT calculations suggested that the experimental values were best described as a low-spin S = 1/2 state (Table 3, vide infra).

The overall S = ½ ground states for both Fe1 and Fe2 prompted additional studies by X-band EPR spectroscopy. The spectrum of Fe1 was recorded at 10K in toluene glass and is presented in Figure 3a. A rhombic signal was observed with gx = 1.56, gy = 1.64 and gz = 3.89, values consistent with a metal-centered spin. By contrast, the spectrum of Fe2, recorded under identical conditions exhibits an axial signal and is frequently observed with low-spin ferric compounds.31-34 EPR simulations as shown in Figure 3 (red line) supported S = 1/2 ground states for the both complexes. While the origin of the shape difference between Figure 3a and b is unclear on current stage, estimated g tensors corroborated that spin density is mainly centered on the metal center. Of note a related ruthenium-based metalloradical exhibited significant delocalization of spin density on the metal center and on the supporting ligand.19

The computational results are consistent with the experimental data obtained from magnetic susceptibility measurements, Mössbauer, and EPR spectroscopy. Indeed, the Mössbauer parameters, such as isomer shift and quadruple splitting, were reasonably reproduced with single point calculations of S = 1/2 states at the TPSS/{CP(PPP) for Fe, def2- TZVP for other atoms} level of theory (Table 3).30 The observed, relatively small quadrupole splitting is attributed to the electronic configuration where minimal valence contribution to electric field gradient is expected.36 Spin density plots of the S = 1/2 states for Fe1 and Fe2 both supported localization of spin on the iron center (Figure 3c), supporting the metal-centered EPR spectra.

Qualitative molecular orbitals are described in Figure 5. Critical canonical orbitals of the diimine ligand include filled σ, filled π1, and unfilled π2 orbitals. Orbital overlap with the [(η5-C5Me5)Fe] fragment, as shown in the center of Figure 5, gave a system consisting of 8 total orbitals with 11 electrons. While dx2-y2, and dz2 orbitals are essentially non-bonding due to a lack of symmetry-allowed counterparts, the dyz and dxz orbitals forms an in-phase and an out-of-phase combination with the diimine π1 and π2 orbitals through the π system, respectively. Consequently, two electrons are filled in a ligand-based (π2 + dxz) orbital, and a metal-based (dxz – π1) orbital becomes the lowest unoccupied molecular orbital (LUMO). A single electron occupies the remaining (dyz – π1) orbital, generating the metalloradical character observed in the experimental measurements and the computational studies. Kohn-Sham orbitals of (dyz – π2) derived from the calculations qualitatively supported this rationalization (Figure 5, inset). It can be concluded that the π-acidic nature of the diimine ligand maximizes the overlap between dxz and

π2, thus leading to two-electron reduction of the ligand π- system.

Having a structural and electronic understanding of the iron compounds, the reactivity towards H2 was explored with the goal of generating the corresponding iron hydrides. Pressurizing a J-Young NMR tube containing a benzene solution of Fe1 or Fe2 with 4 atm of H2 produced no evidence for reaction, as judged by 1H NMR spectroscopy. Irradiation of the mixture with 420 nm LED also resulted in no reaction. Computational analysis provided additional insight into the lack of reactivity. To gauge the feasibility of the reaction, geometry optimizations of hypothetical (η5-C5Me5)Fe(MesDI)H and (η5-C5Me5)Fe(MesPI)H were performed. Singlet, triplet, and quintet spin states were considered to evaluate Fe–H bond dissociation free energies (BDFEs), and the singlet states were identified as the lowest energy. This analysis established that the Fe–H BDFEs for (η5-C5Me5)Fe(MesDI)H and (η5-C5Me5)Fe(MesPI)H were 42.1 and 51.3 kcal/mol, respectively (Figure S7 and S8). Considering hydrogenation of Fp dimer to FpH (BDFE of 63 kcal/mol)37 requires a significant pressure of H2,38 making the desired weaker Fe–H bond by breaking the H–H bond of H2 renders this a practically challenging process under ambient conditions.

## CONCLUSIONS

Iron compounds containing the [η5-C5Me5] anion and dianionic diimine ligand were synthesized and characterized. A straightforward, one-pot procedure from (κ2-N,Nʹ)FeCl2 was developed by chemical reduction with two equivalents of Li[C5Me5]. One-electron reductions of the (κ2- N,Nʹ)Fe(II)Cl2 derivatives were observed, followed by chloride/η5-C5Me5 metathesis yielded more oxidized ferric, (η5- C5Me5)Fe(III)(κ2-N,Nʹ) products. This work provides useful insights on designing and analyzing new ligand scaffolds coordinating Earth-abundant metals and insights into the electronic structure of metalloradicals.
